title: Lowering a test cutoff: higher sensitivity
vignette: A novel serum biomarker, UWRLD99, is being evaluated for early detection of pancreatic cancer. The concentration of UWRLD99 (measured in international units [IU] per dL) has been found to be elevated in patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Test results in 200 volunteers ("healthy") and 190 patients with biopsy-proven pancreatic cancer ("diseased") are shown as two overlapping bell-shaped distributions: the healthy curve is centered at a lower UWRLD99 level and the diseased curve at a higher level, with values above the cutoff called positive. The investigators first determined sensitivity and specificity using a cutoff of 200 IU/dL. If they had instead used a lower cutoff (shifting the threshold to the left, toward the healthy curve), which of the following would most likely be seen?

clues.text: elevated in patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma
clues.note: This orients the curves: higher marker = disease. So the diseased distribution sits to the RIGHT, and moving the cutoff left/right changes who is called positive.
The overlap between healthy and diseased is exactly why moving the cutoff trades sensitivity against specificity - no single threshold cleanly separates the groups.

clues.text: lower cutoff (shifting the threshold to the left, toward the healthy curve)
clues.note: Lowering the cutoff calls MORE people positive. More truly diseased test positive (true positives up, false negatives down) -> higher sensitivity; but more healthy also test positive (false positives up) -> lower specificity.

whatMatters: Lowering the cutoff (threshold to the left) labels MORE people positive. That captures more truly diseased patients (more true positives, fewer false negatives) = HIGHER SENSITIVITY, at the cost of more false positives (lower specificity). Answer C. (A is backwards - false negatives fall; D is backwards - false positives rise; E is backwards - true positives rise.)
strategy: Anchor the rule: LOW cutoff -> high sensitivity (SnNout, good for screening); HIGH cutoff -> high specificity (SpPin, good for confirmation). With 'diseased = higher values,' moving the line LEFT reclassifies borderline patients as positive: true positives rise, false negatives fall (sensitivity up), and false positives rise (specificity down). Then reject each reversed distractor.

eliminations.label: Higher false negatives - reversed, your pick
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: false negatives are diseased people who test negative. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a LOWER cutoff calls more diseased people positive, so false negatives DECREASE (that's why sensitivity rises). This is the exact reversal of what happens. ✅ Correct if: the cutoff were RAISED.

eliminations.label: Higher positive predictive value - prevalence-dependent
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: PPV = TP/(TP+FP), the chance a positive is truly diseased. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a lower cutoff raises BOTH TP and FP; with more false positives, PPV generally FALLS (and PPV depends on prevalence, not given). ✅ Correct if: prevalence rose or a more specific cutoff were used.

eliminations.label: Lower false positives - reversed
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: false positives are healthy people who test positive. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: shifting the cutoff left into the healthy curve calls MORE healthy people positive, so false positives INCREASE (specificity falls). ✅ Correct if: the cutoff were RAISED.

eliminations.label: Lower true positives - reversed
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: true positives are diseased people who test positive. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a lower cutoff makes MORE diseased people test positive, so true positives INCREASE. ✅ Correct if: the cutoff were RAISED (fewer positives overall).

reasoning: Diseased patients have higher marker values (diseased curve on the right)
Lowering the cutoff labels more people positive
More truly diseased become positive -> true positives up, false negatives down -> sensitivity up
(False positives also rise -> specificity down); answer C (higher sensitivity)
mechanism: For a quantitative test with overlapping healthy and diseased distributions, the cutoff sets the positive/negative boundary. Because diseased individuals have higher UWRLD99 values, moving the cutoff to a LOWER value reclassifies more people (both diseased and healthy) as positive. Among the diseased, more now test positive - true positives increase and false negatives decrease - so SENSITIVITY (TP/[TP+FN]) rises. Among the healthy, more also test positive - false positives increase and true negatives decrease - so SPECIFICITY (TN/[TN+FP]) falls. Positive predictive value depends on disease prevalence and generally declines as false positives rise. This is the classic sensitivity-specificity trade-off: a low cutoff maximizes sensitivity (good for screening; SnNout), whereas a high cutoff maximizes specificity (good for confirmation; SpPin).

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Biostat > sensitivity/specificity, PPV/NPV, and the cutoff trade-off (SnNout vs SpPin); 2x2 table definitions of TP/FP/FN/TN.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: Translate 'lower cutoff' into direction of TP/FP/FN. Lower threshold = more positives = more TP and FP, fewer FN.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on sensitivity, specificity, PPV, false negative vs false positive, or 'cutoff/threshold'? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: A, D, and E are exact reversals (they describe RAISING the cutoff). B (PPV) depends on prevalence and usually falls as false positives rise.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.message: On the two-curve figure, the diseased curve is on the right; a line moved LEFT crosses into more of both curves -> more positives (more TP and FP). Anchor: 'lower line = more positives = higher sensitivity.'

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: lower cutoff -> up sensitivity, up false positives, down false negatives, down specificity (SnNout); raise cutoff for the opposite (SpPin).

keywords.back: Sensitive test, Negative rules OUT (good for screening)
